slides.title: The Complex Plane As A Geometric Coordinate System
slides.notes: Open the lecture by presenting complex numbers as a language for geometry, not as an algebra detour. The course will later study inversions, Mobius maps, disk models, and quotient spaces; this chapter supplies the coordinate habits needed for those objects. Emphasize that every formula on the deck has a visual check attached to it.

slides.title: Route Through The Chapter
slides.notes: This route is useful because it separates four roles that students often blend together. A complex number can be a point, a displacement, a multiplier, or a constraint variable. Keep asking which role is active. That question prevents many later errors, especially when the same algebraic expression appears in a transformation or a locus equation.

slides.title: Addition Is Displacement
slides.notes: Use the generated figure to make addition feel like moving an arrow rather than applying a rule to two coordinates. The subtraction vector is especially important: it is the displacement from one point to another. That displacement language will later become the natural way to discuss distances, angle quotients, and transformations of small local configurations.

slides.title: Modulus Measures Length; Conjugation Reflects
slides.notes: This slide turns two algebraic operations into two visible measurements. The modulus is the length of the radius vector, while conjugation is a mirror operation across the real axis. Stress the product identity because it lets students verify numerical work and later recognize circle equations written with \(z\overline z\).

slides.title: Polar Form Separates Size From Direction
slides.notes: Pause on the phrase modulo a full turn. Students can compute an arctangent and still lose the quadrant or forget that adding \(2\pi\) gives the same direction. The converter figure should be read as two coordinate systems for the same point, not as a new kind of point. This distinction is the bridge to multiplication.

slides.title: Multiplication Is Rotation Plus Scale
slides.notes: This is the conceptual center of the chapter. Multiplication by a fixed nonzero complex number is a similarity of the plane: it scales all distances by one factor and rotates all directions by one angle. Present the formula after the picture so that the algebra explains the visual behavior rather than replacing it.

slides.title: Division Reverses The Similarity
slides.notes: Division is best taught as undoing multiplication. The reciprocal reverses both pieces of the similarity: the scale becomes \(1/\rho\), and the angle changes sign. The conjugate formula is not merely a computational trick; it converts division into multiplication by a reflected vector divided by a real length square.

slides.title: Quotients Measure Oriented Angles
slides.notes: The oriented angle formula is a compact example of the chapter's philosophy. Subtraction creates vectors based at the same point, division compares them, and the argument extracts the turn. Ask students to identify the geometric job of each operation. This prevents the formula from feeling mysterious or memorized.

slides.title: Equations Become Geometric Sets
slides.notes: This slide turns algebraic constraints into visible subsets. The important teaching move is to name the measurement being fixed: distance from a center, horizontal coordinate, vertical coordinate, or direction from the origin. Later chapters will use this same translation when clines, disks, and boundary identifications appear in more sophisticated models.

slides.title: Executable Checks Keep The Geometry Honest
slides.notes: Use this slide to explain why the notebook saves checks instead of only saving pictures. The computation tests whether two descriptions of multiplication agree, and the figure statistics test whether the visual artifacts actually contain information. These checks are small, but they model the discipline students should bring to later geometry notebooks.

slides.title: Three Pitfalls To Name Explicitly
slides.notes: This pitfall slide is meant to be practical. Students should leave with concrete repair strategies: state the branch, expand multiplication once to see the cross terms, and translate conjugate expressions into real coordinates. These habits keep the complex plane from becoming symbol manipulation detached from geometry.

slides.title: The Complex Plane Is A Working Geometry Lab
slides.notes: Close by connecting this short chapter to the rest of the course. The complex plane is not the final geometric setting; it is the coordinate system that makes later settings computable. Students should be able to explain one artifact in their own words by naming the model, the operation, and the visible evidence for the claimed measurement.
